disease.name: Influenza

overview.definition: Influenza is an acute febrile respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses, characterized by abrupt onset of fever, headache, myalgia, malaise, cough, sore throat, and rhinitis, with the potential to cause severe complications including pneumonia, ARDS, and death — especially in high-risk populations.

global_burden.us_annual_burden: 9–41 million illnesses, 140,000–710,000 hospitalizations, and 12,000–52,000 deaths per year (CDC)
global_burden.high_risk_group: Children under 5, adults over 65, pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals, and those with chronic medical conditions
global_burden.economic_burden: Significant loss of productivity; hundreds of millions in healthcare costs annually

seasonality.tropical_regions: Year-round circulation with less distinct seasonality
seasonality.cause_of_seasonality: Cold dry air preserves viral particles longer; people spend more time indoors; vitamin D deficiency in winter may reduce immune responses

pandemic_history.name: 1918 Spanish Flu
pandemic_history.note: Deadliest pandemic in recorded history; unusually severe mortality in young adults (20–40 years)

pandemic_history.name: 2009 H1N1 Pandemic (Swine Flu)
pandemic_history.note: Unusual severity in younger adults; elderly had partial immunity from 1918-related strains; now circulates as seasonal influenza

anatomy_and_physiology.overview: Influenza virus infects ciliated respiratory epithelial cells via hemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors. Viral replication destroys the epithelial lining, triggering innate immune responses. Systemic symptoms (fever, myalgia, fatigue) are primarily immune-mediated via cytokines rather than direct viral invasion of systemic tissues.

phase_1_infection_and_replication.description: Virus infects upper respiratory tract epithelium; incubation phase; innate immune activation begins; type I interferon (IFN-α/β) production initiated
phase_1_infection_and_replication.viral_tropism: Ciliated columnar epithelium of nasal passages, trachea, bronchi; type I and II pneumocytes in severe disease
phase_1_infection_and_replication.tissue_destruction: Viral replication destroys cilia and epithelial cells; impairs mucociliary clearance; creates portal for secondary bacterial infections

phase_2_immune_response.description: Innate immune response: neutrophils and macrophages infiltrate respiratory mucosa; cytokine production causes systemic symptoms
phase_2_immune_response.systemic_symptoms_mechanism: Cytokines (especially TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-α) cause fever, myalgia, fatigue, and headache — not direct viral invasion of muscles or brain
phase_2_immune_response.lymphocyte_response: T-cell and B-cell adaptive immunity develops within 5–10 days; antibodies to HA and NA key to clearance and protection

phase_3_complications.primary_viral_pneumonia: Direct viral pneumonia from influenza replication in alveolar epithelium; bilateral patchy infiltrates; high mortality; less common than secondary bacterial pneumonia
phase_3_complications.secondary_bacterial_pneumonia: Most common severe complication; destruction of ciliated epithelium allows bacterial colonization; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes most common organisms; may occur 3–7 days after initial improvement
phase_3_complications.cytokine_dysregulation: Severe influenza can trigger dysregulated cytokine response; exaggerated inflammatory response contributes to ARDS and multi-organ dysfunction
phase_3_complications.cardiovascular: Influenza infection triggers acute MI via plaque destabilization, hypercoagulable state, and direct myocardial inflammation; risk of MI increases 3–5x in week after flu diagnosis
phase_3_complications.neurological: Rare but includes encephalitis, acute necrotizing encephalopathy, febrile seizures; especially in children

influenza_A.description: Most clinically significant type; causes seasonal epidemics and all major pandemics; infects humans, birds, pigs, horses, seals, and other animals
influenza_A.classification: Classified by hemagglutinin (H1–H18) and neuraminidase (N1–N11) subtypes
influenza_A.reservoir: Wild aquatic birds are the natural reservoir; pigs are important mixing vessels for reassortment

influenza_B.description: Causes seasonal epidemics; primarily infects humans; milder than Type A; does not cause pandemics
lineages: B/Yamagata lineage (no longer detected as of 2020; removed from quadrivalent vaccines)
influenza_B.note: Children are more severely affected by Type B than adults

influenza_C.description: Causes mild respiratory illness; rarely causes epidemics; less clinical significance; infects humans and pigs
influenza_C.severity: Usually mild; does not require specific antiviral treatment

influenza_D.description: Primarily infects cattle; no documented human infections; not a current human health concern

uncomplicated.definition: Influenza illness involving the upper respiratory tract and/or lower respiratory tract without evidence of complications
uncomplicated.symptoms: Fever, cough, sore throat, rhinitis, headache, myalgia, fatigue
uncomplicated.management: Outpatient supportive care; antiviral therapy for high-risk patients within 2 days of onset

complicated.definition: Influenza with evidence of lower respiratory tract disease, central nervous system involvement, significant dehydration, bacterial superinfection, or exacerbation of underlying chronic conditions
complicated.management: Hospitalization; antiviral therapy (oseltamivir preferred); monitor for secondary bacterial infection

severe.definition: Requiring ICU admission; respiratory failure; hemodynamic instability; multi-organ involvement
severe.management: ICU care; invasive mechanical ventilation if needed; corticosteroids only for specific indications; broad-spectrum antibiotics if secondary bacterial pneumonia

causes: Infection with influenza type A viruses (H1N1, H3N2 — responsible for most seasonal epidemics)
Infection with influenza type B viruses (B/Victoria lineage — primarily affects children and young adults)
Infection with influenza type C virus (mild, rare)
Zoonotic infection with avian influenza (H5N1, H7N9) from direct animal contact
Hemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors on respiratory epithelial cells initiating viral entry
Viral replication within ciliated respiratory epithelium causing cell death and inflammation
Cytokine-mediated systemic inflammatory response producing fever, myalgia, and fatigue
Antigenic drift enabling seasonal strain to evade pre-existing immunity from prior infection or vaccination

transmission.primary_mode: Respiratory droplets expelled during talking, coughing, or sneezing by infected individuals

routes.description: Large droplets (>5 µm) travel short distances (<1–2 meters); land on mucous membranes of eyes, nose, or mouth of susceptible persons; most common route
Fine droplet nuclei (<5 µm) can remain suspended in air in enclosed spaces; particularly relevant in crowded indoor settings; evidence for airborne transmission increasing
Touching contaminated surfaces (doorknobs, phones, keyboards) then touching nose, mouth, or eyes; influenza virus survives on hard surfaces up to 24 hours

transmission.contagious_period: From 1 day before symptom onset to 5–7 days after becoming ill; children and immunocompromised individuals may shed virus for longer
transmission.incubation_details: Influenza is most contagious in the first 2–3 days of illness when viral shedding is highest
high_risk_settings: Long-term care facilities and nursing homes
Crowded indoor spaces with poor ventilation

zoonotic_transmission.avian_influenza_H5N1: Transmitted to humans through direct contact with infected poultry, surfaces contaminated with feces/secretions; extremely limited human-to-human transmission
zoonotic_transmission.swine_influenza: Transmission from pigs to humans possible; 2009 H1N1 pandemic originated from swine-origin reassortant virus
zoonotic_transmission.risk_settings: Poultry farms, live animal markets, slaughterhouses

incubation_period.onset_character: Abrupt; flu symptoms typically develop suddenly and can be severe within hours of onset
incubation_period.note: Shorter incubation (1–2 days) is common; distinguishes flu from many other respiratory infections with longer incubation periods

primary_symptoms: Sudden onset of fever or feeling feverish/chills (38–40°C / 100.4–104°F)
Severe muscle aches and body pains (myalgia)
Watery or red eyes (conjunctivitis — less common)
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Oxygen saturation below 92% on room air
Signs of dehydration (no urination for 8+ hours, dry mouth, dizziness)
Bluish discoloration of lips or fingernails (cyanosis)
High fever above 40°C (104°F) unresponsive to antipyretics
Severe weakness or inability to stand
In children: fast breathing or labored breathing, ribs showing with each breath, grayish skin color, not drinking fluids
Symptoms that improve then return with fever and worsening cough (sign of secondary bacterial pneumonia)

risk_factors.details: Highest hospitalization and death rates among infants <6 months; immature immune system; high-risk group for severe complications
All children under 5 considered at increased risk for serious flu complications; highest incidence of influenza illness
Immunosenescence; highest hospitalization and mortality rates; responsible for >90% of influenza deaths in the US; attenuated vaccine response

risk_factors.factor: Pregnancy (all trimesters) and up to 2 weeks postpartum
risk_factors.details: Physiological immunomodulation; reduced lung capacity; increased risk of hospitalization, ICU admission, preterm birth, and maternal death; influenza vaccination strongly recommended
Influenza triggers severe asthma and COPD exacerbations; impaired mucociliary clearance; high risk of pneumonia
Heart disease (excluding hypertension alone); influenza increases MI risk 3–5x; heart failure worsened by fluid shifts and hypoxemia
Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil and macrophage function; higher risk of secondary bacterial pneumonia and hospitalization
Uremia impairs immune function; higher complication and hospitalization rates
Impaired immune function and coagulation; higher risk of severe influenza
Includes cerebral palsy, epilepsy, stroke, intellectual disability, muscular dystrophy, spinal cord injury; impaired airway clearance; higher aspiration risk
Vascular and pulmonary complications worsened by influenza infection; high-risk group per CDC/IDSA
Obesity (BMI ≥ 40 — morbid obesity) significantly increases risk of severe influenza and hospitalization; impaired respiratory mechanics; pro-inflammatory state

HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, cancer patients on chemotherapy, patients on high-dose corticosteroids or biological therapies; markedly impaired influenza-specific immunity; higher viral loads and prolonged shedding
Strongest modifiable risk factor for influenza-related hospitalization and death; annual vaccination significantly reduces risk

risk_factors.factor: Residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities
risk_factors.details: High concentration of elderly and frail individuals; close quarters facilitate rapid spread; institutional outbreaks common

risk_factors.factor: Children aged <19 years on long-term aspirin therapy
risk_factors.details: Risk of Reye's syndrome if given aspirin during influenza infection; aspirin must be avoided; acetaminophen or ibuprofen preferred
Higher hospitalization rates for influenza compared to white populations; CDC high-priority group for vaccination
Damages respiratory epithelium and cilia; impairs mucociliary clearance; increases severity of influenza

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects influenza A and B viral nucleoprotein antigens in respiratory specimens; results in 10–15 minutes
diagnostic_tests.specimen: Nasopharyngeal swab, nasal swab, or nasal wash
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity: 50–70% (variable; low sensitivity means negative results do not exclude flu)
diagnostic_tests.who_2024_recommendation: Digital immunoassay (DIA) preferred over traditional RIDTs for non-severe cases; DIA has higher sensitivity (~80%) than traditional RIDTs
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Cannot distinguish influenza subtypes; negative result does not rule out flu — treat based on clinical judgment

diagnostic_tests.method: RT-PCR (Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction) / NAAT
diagnostic_tests.description: Detects influenza viral RNA; most sensitive and specific test; can identify and subtype influenza A and B; can distinguish seasonal from pandemic strains
diagnostic_tests.specimen: Nasopharyngeal swab (reference standard); nasal swab; bronchoalveolar lavage in severe disease
diagnostic_tests.turnaround_time: 2–8 hours in laboratory; 30–60 minutes for point-of-care platforms
diagnostic_tests.who_2024_recommendation: NAAT recommended for diagnosing suspected SEVERE influenza and for all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza

diagnostic_tests.description: Simultaneously tests for influenza A, influenza B, and other respiratory pathogens (RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, adenovirus, etc.) in one assay
diagnostic_tests.clinical_role: Preferred for hospitalized patients; differentiates influenza from COVID-19 and other co-circulating respiratory viruses
diagnostic_tests.authority: CDC and IDSA recommend for hospitalized patients with severe respiratory illness

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects influenza viral antigens in respiratory epithelial cells using fluorescently labelled antibodies; distinguishes influenza A and B
diagnostic_tests.clinical_role: Useful when rapid PCR not available; less commonly used now

diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard for virus isolation and characterization; grows live virus in cell culture (MDCK cells) or embryonated eggs
diagnostic_tests.clinical_role: Not used for acute diagnosis; used for public health surveillance, antiviral resistance testing, vaccine strain selection
diagnostic_tests.authority: WHO GISRS (Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System) uses viral culture for global monitoring

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects influenza-specific antibodies (paired acute and convalescent serum showing ≥4-fold rise in HI titer confirms infection)
diagnostic_tests.timing: Requires 2 serum samples taken 2–4 weeks apart; not useful for acute diagnosis
diagnostic_tests.clinical_role: Epidemiological surveillance; research; not for acute clinical diagnosis

diagnostic_tests.description: Reveals bilateral patchy infiltrates or consolidation in influenza pneumonia; may be normal in uncomplicated influenza
diagnostic_tests.clinical_role: Indicated for patients with dyspnea, hypoxemia, or suspected pneumonia; not needed for uncomplicated flu
diagnostic_tests.finding: Bilateral interstitial or patchy alveolar infiltrates; lobar consolidation if secondary bacterial pneumonia

diagnostic_tests.description: Reveals leukopenia (low white cell count) and lymphopenia in uncomplicated influenza; leukocytosis with neutrophilia suggests secondary bacterial infection

typical_findings.WBC: Normal or low (leukopenia in early viral phase)
typical_findings.note: High WBC/neutrophilia should raise suspicion of bacterial superinfection

diagnostic_tests.description: Used to assess severity in hospitalized patients

key_markers.CRP: Elevated in influenza pneumonia; very high CRP suggests secondary bacterial infection
key_markers.procalcitonin: Low/normal in pure viral influenza; elevated if bacterial superinfection; helps guide antibiotic decisions
key_markers.LDH: Elevated in severe influenza with extensive tissue destruction

diagnostic_tests.description: Monitors peripheral oxygen saturation; SpO2 < 92% indicates significant hypoxemia; home monitoring recommended in high-risk patients
diagnostic_tests.clinical_importance: Identify early respiratory decompensation; guide oxygen supplementation

treatment_options.description: Most healthy adults and children recover from uncomplicated influenza with supportive care only
interventions: Rest and avoid strenuous activity during febrile illness
Stay home to prevent spread to others
Adequate hydration — water, broths, herbal teas, oral rehydration solutions (2–3 liters daily)
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen for fever, headache, and myalgia — NOT aspirin (except adults; never in children due to Reye's syndrome risk)
Warm saline gargles for sore throat
Nasal decongestants or saline nasal rinse for congestion
Honey and warm fluids for cough (adults and children over 1 year)
Monitor for worsening; seek care if symptoms do not improve after 5 days or worsen

treatment_options.description: Patients with risk factors for severe disease should receive antiviral therapy as early as possible — within 2 days of symptom onset for best effect
interventions: Oral oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — preferred for high-risk outpatients with suspected/confirmed influenza
Oral baloxavir marboxil (Xofluza) — conditionally recommended within 2 days for high-risk patients (WHO 2024)
Inhaled zanamivir or IV peramivir as alternatives based on age and contraindications (CDC 2025)
Supportive care as above
Close monitoring for complications
Antiviral treatment recommended even if >48 hours since symptom onset in high-risk patients with progressive disease (CDC)

treatment_options.setting: Complicated — Hospitalized with Pneumonia or Lower Respiratory Involvement
treatment_options.description: Patients with complications require hospital admission and aggressive treatment
interventions: IV oseltamivir or oral oseltamivir (preferred antiviral; start regardless of time since symptom onset)
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 94%
IV fluids if dehydrated or unable to take orally
Antibiotics if secondary bacterial pneumonia suspected (based on WBC, procalcitonin, CXR consolidation) — amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftriaxone, or based on local antibiogram
Blood cultures and sputum cultures before antibiotics
Monitor inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin, CBC) daily
Deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis (LMWH)

treatment_options.description: Patients with respiratory failure, ARDS, or hemodynamic instability require intensive care
interventions: IV oseltamivir 75–150 mg twice daily (higher dose considered in severe disease)
Invasive mechanical ventilation for ARDS (lung-protective: low tidal volume 6 mL/kg IBW)
High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) or NIV as bridge before intubation
Prone positioning for severe ARDS
Vasopressors for septic shock
Corticosteroids only for ARDS per WHO 2024 recommendations (NOT recommended routinely; may worsen outcomes)
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for secondary bacterial pneumonia (Staphylococcal MRSA coverage if needed)
ECMO for refractory ARDS in specialized centers
Renal replacement therapy for AKI

treatment_options.description: Antivirals can prevent influenza after exposure — recommended for high-risk individuals exposed within 48 hours
interventions: Oseltamivir 75 mg once daily for 10 days post-exposure (WHO 2024 conditional recommendation for high-risk individuals)
Baloxavir, zanamivir, or laninamivir as alternatives (WHO 2024)
Not recommended for routine use or as a substitute for vaccination
Consider for unvaccinated high-risk individuals exposed to confirmed influenza within 48 hours
Institutional outbreak management: treat all residents/staff with antivirals (CDC/IDSA)

vaccination.overview: Annual influenza vaccination is the single most effective strategy to prevent influenza illness, hospitalization, and death. Vaccines are reformulated each year to match predicted circulating strains.
vaccination.who_should_get_vaccinated: Everyone aged ≥6 months (CDC 2025); priority groups include elderly (≥65), children (6 months–5 years), pregnant women, healthcare workers, immunocompromised individuals, and people with chronic medical conditions
vaccination.timing: Ideally before the start of flu season (by end of October in northern hemisphere); vaccination at any time during flu season still beneficial

vaccine_types.mechanism: Contains killed influenza virus antigens; stimulates antibody response without causing infection
vaccine_types.notes: Standard recommendation for most people including pregnant women and immunocompromised

vaccine_types.mechanism: Contains 4x the antigen dose of standard IIV; generates stronger immune response in elderly with reduced immunogenicity
vaccine_types.notes: Preferred for adults ≥65 years; superior protection vs standard dose

vaccine_types.mechanism: Contains MF59 adjuvant (oil-in-water emulsion) to enhance immune response; particularly useful in elderly
vaccine_types.notes: Alternative to high-dose for adults ≥65 years

vaccine_types.mechanism: Produced using recombinant DNA technology; does not use eggs; higher HA content
vaccine_types.notes: Safe for egg-allergic individuals; preferred by some clinicians for immunocompromised

vaccine_types.mechanism: Contains weakened live virus; administered intranasally; stimulates both mucosal and systemic immunity; may provide broader immune response
contraindications: Children 2–4 with wheezing or asthma history

vaccination.vaccine_composition: Quadrivalent vaccines contain two influenza A strains (H1N1 and H3N2) and one or two influenza B strains; selected by WHO GISRS twice yearly (February for northern hemisphere; September for southern hemisphere) based on circulating strains

vaccine_effectiveness.typical_range: 40–60% against influenza A; higher against influenza B
vaccine_effectiveness.variability: Depends on match between vaccine strains and circulating strains; higher in well-matched seasons
vaccine_effectiveness.severe_disease: More effective at preventing hospitalization and death (70–85%) than preventing all symptomatic illness
vaccine_effectiveness.cardiovascular_benefit: Vaccination reduces risk of MI by 15–30% in high-risk cardiac patients (multiple studies)

antivirals_for_prophylaxis: Oseltamivir 75 mg once daily (post-exposure: 10 days; seasonal: up to 6 weeks)
Baloxavir (single dose or repeated dosing — under study)
indications: High-risk individuals exposed to confirmed influenza within 48 hours who are unvaccinated or received vaccine <2 weeks ago
Institutional outbreaks in nursing homes — treat all residents and staff
Immunocompromised individuals who may not respond to vaccination
Pregnant women in high-transmission settings when vaccination contraindicated
chemoprophylaxis.authority: WHO 2024 conditionally recommends post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk individuals; IDSA 2018 guidelines

non_pharmaceutical_interventions.evidence: Very strong — single most effective preventive measure
non_pharmaceutical_interventions.details: All persons ≥6 months annually; priority for high-risk groups
Wash hands with soap and water for ≥20 seconds especially after coughing/sneezing, before eating, after touching surfaces in public; use alcohol-based sanitizer (≥60% ethanol) when soap unavailable
Cover mouth and nose with tissue or inner elbow when coughing or sneezing; discard tissue immediately; wash hands; reduces droplet spread
Stay home for at least 24 hours after fever has resolved without fever-reducing medications; reduces community transmission; critical for preventing spread in workplaces and schools

non_pharmaceutical_interventions.measure: Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth
non_pharmaceutical_interventions.details: Reduces fomite transmission; influenza virus survives on surfaces up to 24 hours
Surgical mask or N95 respirator reduces influenza transmission; especially recommended for healthcare workers, high-risk patients in crowded settings during peak flu season
Disinfect high-touch surfaces (doorknobs, phones, keyboards) with household disinfectants; influenza virus inactivated by 70% ethanol, 1% hydrogen peroxide, common household bleach solutions
Increase outdoor air ventilation in schools, workplaces, and healthcare settings; HEPA air purifiers; CO2 monitoring

non_pharmaceutical_interventions.measure: Avoid close contact with sick people
non_pharmaceutical_interventions.details: Maintain distance from people with flu symptoms; especially important for high-risk individuals

complications.name: Primary Viral Pneumonia
complications.description: Direct extension of influenza virus into lower respiratory tract (alveoli); bilateral patchy infiltrates; high mortality; more common with pandemic strains; less common than secondary bacterial pneumonia

complications.name: Secondary Bacterial Pneumonia
complications.description: Most common severe complication; influenza destroys ciliated epithelium creating portal for bacterial infection 3–7 days after initial viral illness; classic pattern: initial improvement then relapse with worsening fever and productive cough; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes most common organisms
complications.note: MRSA co-infection particularly dangerous; high mortality

complications.name: Mixed Viral-Bacterial Pneumonia
complications.description: Simultaneous viral and bacterial pneumonia; combination of both patterns; significant mortality

complications.name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
complications.description: Bilateral lung injury with refractory hypoxemia; complication of severe viral or secondary bacterial pneumonia; requires ICU and mechanical ventilation

complications.name: Exacerbation of Asthma
complications.description: Influenza is the most common trigger of severe asthma exacerbations; can require emergency hospitalization

complications.name: Exacerbation of COPD
complications.description: Influenza triggers acute COPD exacerbations with increased mucus, bronchospasm, and hypoxemia

complications.name: Croup (in children)
complications.description: Influenza A and B are common causes of viral croup in children; laryngotracheobronchitis with characteristic barking cough and stridor

complications.name: Acute Myocardial Infarction (MI)
complications.description: Influenza infection increases MI risk 3–5x in the week following diagnosis; mechanisms include plaque destabilization, hypercoagulable state, direct cardiac inflammation, and hypoxemia-induced demand ischemia
complications.prevention: Influenza vaccination significantly reduces risk of MI in high-risk cardiac patients

complications.name: Myocarditis and Pericarditis
complications.description: Rare; direct viral inflammation of heart muscle; presents with chest pain, elevated troponin, ECG changes

complications.name: Worsening of Congestive Heart Failure
complications.description: Influenza triggers acute decompensated heart failure in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease

complications.name: Febrile Seizures
complications.description: Most common neurological complication in children aged 6 months to 5 years; high fever triggers seizure; usually benign and self-limiting

complications.name: Influenza-Associated Encephalitis / Encephalopathy
complications.description: Rare but serious; altered consciousness, seizures, behavioral changes; can occur without direct viral brain invasion; cytokine-mediated; acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE) in children

complications.name: Reye's Syndrome
complications.description: Rare but life-threatening hepatic encephalopathy in children given aspirin during viral illness (especially influenza or varicella); presents with vomiting, confusion, liver failure; prevented by avoiding aspirin in children
complications.prevention: Complete avoidance of aspirin in patients under 18 years with suspected viral illness

complications.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
complications.description: Rare post-infectious autoimmune peripheral neuropathy; ascending muscle weakness; can follow influenza infection

complications.name: Otitis Media (Ear Infection)
complications.description: Very common in children with influenza; bacteria colonize Eustachian tube after viral damage; ear pain, hearing loss; treated with antibiotics if bacterial

complications.name: Sinusitis
complications.description: Secondary bacterial sinusitis following influenza; nasal congestion → sinus obstruction → bacterial overgrowth; facial pain, purulent discharge

complications: Congenital abnormalities (associated with high fever in first trimester)

complications.name: Post-Influenza Fatigue Syndrome
complications.description: Persistent fatigue, weakness, and malaise lasting weeks to months after acute influenza; more common in elderly; impairs return to normal activity
complications.severity: Mild to moderate; self-limiting in most cases

disease.when_to_see_doctor: Seek medical evaluation promptly if you are in a high-risk group (age ≥65, child <5 years, pregnant, immunocompromised, or have chronic heart, lung, kidney, liver, metabolic, or neurological conditions) and develop flu symptoms — early antiviral treatment within 48 hours significantly reduces severity. You should also see a doctor if symptoms are unusually severe from onset, if you are not improving after 5 days, if fever returns after initial improvement (possible secondary bacterial pneumonia), if you develop difficulty breathing, or if you are unsure whether you need antiviral treatment. Patients with asthma or COPD should contact their doctor immediately as influenza triggers severe exacerbations requiring urgent medication adjustment.
emergency_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Persistent chest pain or pressure
Oxygen saturation below 92% on room air
Confusion or altered mental status
Severe or persistent vomiting
Signs of dehydration (no urination for 8+ hours, dry mouth, dizziness)
Bluish discoloration of lips or fingernails (cyanosis)
Seizures
High fever above 40°C (104°F) unresponsive to antipyretics
Severe weakness or inability to stand
In children: fast breathing or labored breathing, ribs showing with each breath, grayish skin color, not drinking fluids
Symptoms that improve then return with fever and worsening cough (sign of secondary bacterial pneumonia)

raw_source_backup.description: Influenza (flu) is a highly contagious acute respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses (types A, B, C, and D) that primarily infect the nose, throat, and lungs, producing a sudden onset of fever, chills, headache, severe myalgia, and respiratory symptoms. The disease causes approximately 1 billion infections annually worldwide, including 3–5 million severe cases and 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths, with epidemics occurring seasonally — primarily in winter months — driven by continuous antigenic drift and periodic antigenic shift of the virus. Influenza A viruses are the most clinically significant, responsible for all recorded influenza pandemics including the devastating 1918 Spanish flu, the 1957 and 1968 pandemics, and the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, with annual vaccination remaining the cornerstone of prevention.

causative_agent.type: RNA virus — enveloped, negative-sense, segmented, single-stranded RNA

hemagglutinin_HA.function: Binds to sialic acid receptors on host respiratory epithelial cells; initiates viral entry; primary target of neutralizing antibodies and vaccines
hemagglutinin_HA.host_specificity: Human strains bind alpha-2,6-linked sialic acid (upper respiratory tract); avian strains bind alpha-2,3-linked sialic acid (lower respiratory tract and GI tract in birds)
hemagglutinin_HA.clinical_importance: Changes in HA allow viruses to evade pre-existing immunity; basis of antigenic drift

neuraminidase_NA.function: Cleaves sialic acid to release newly formed virions from infected cells; facilitates virus spread through respiratory tract mucus; target of antiviral drugs (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir, baloxavir indirectly)
neuraminidase_NA.clinical_importance: Mutations in NA (e.g., H274Y/H275Y) confer resistance to neuraminidase inhibitors

matrix_protein_M2.function: Ion channel; involved in viral uncoating; target of adamantane antivirals (amantadine, rimantadine) — now largely resistant
matrix_protein_M2.resistance_note: Widespread adamantane resistance in circulating H3N2 and H1N1pdm09; adamantanes no longer recommended

PB2_polymerase.function: Viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; target of baloxavir marboxil (cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor)

antigenic_drift.definition: Gradual accumulation of point mutations in HA and NA genes during viral replication; results in small but progressive changes in surface proteins
antigenic_drift.mechanism: RNA polymerase lacks proofreading ability; introduces random mutations; those that evade immunity are selected
antigenic_drift.clinical_consequence: Reduced effectiveness of existing immunity and vaccines; drives need for annual vaccine reformulation

antigenic_shift.definition: Sudden, major change in influenza A surface proteins through genetic reassortment (mixing of gene segments between two different influenza strains co-infecting the same cell)
antigenic_shift.mechanism: Segmented genome allows exchange of whole gene segments; can produce a novel HA or NA subtype
antigenic_shift.clinical_consequence: Creates new pandemic strains with no or minimal existing human immunity; responsible for 1957, 1968, and 2009 pandemics

virus_replication_cycle.step_1: Hemagglutinin binds to sialic acid receptors on respiratory epithelial cells
virus_replication_cycle.step_2: Virus is endocytosed into the cell
virus_replication_cycle.step_3: M2 ion channels acidify the endosome, triggering viral uncoating and release of viral RNA segments into nucleus
virus_replication_cycle.step_4: Viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) replicates viral RNA and transcribes mRNA in the nucleus
virus_replication_cycle.step_5: Viral proteins synthesized in cytoplasm; assembled at cell membrane
virus_replication_cycle.step_6: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release new virions from cell surface
virus_replication_cycle.step_7: New virions infect neighboring cells; spread throughout respiratory tract
virus_replication_cycle.key_target_cells: Ciliated columnar epithelial cells of upper and lower respiratory tract; type I and II alveolar pneumocytes in severe disease

transmission.primary_mode: Respiratory droplets expelled during talking, coughing, or sneezing by infected individuals

routes.description: Large droplets (>5 µm) travel short distances (<1–2 meters); land on mucous membranes of eyes, nose, or mouth of susceptible persons; most common route
Fine droplet nuclei (<5 µm) can remain suspended in air in enclosed spaces; particularly relevant in crowded indoor settings; evidence for airborne transmission increasing
Touching contaminated surfaces (doorknobs, phones, keyboards) then touching nose, mouth, or eyes; influenza virus survives on hard surfaces up to 24 hours

transmission.contagious_period: From 1 day before symptom onset to 5–7 days after becoming ill; children and immunocompromised individuals may shed virus for longer
transmission.incubation_details: Influenza is most contagious in the first 2–3 days of illness when viral shedding is highest
high_risk_settings: Long-term care facilities and nursing homes
Crowded indoor spaces with poor ventilation

zoonotic_transmission.avian_influenza_H5N1: Transmitted to humans through direct contact with infected poultry, surfaces contaminated with feces/secretions; extremely limited human-to-human transmission
zoonotic_transmission.swine_influenza: Transmission from pigs to humans possible; 2009 H1N1 pandemic originated from swine-origin reassortant virus
zoonotic_transmission.risk_settings: Poultry farms, live animal markets, slaughterhouses

incubation_period.onset_character: Abrupt; flu symptoms typically develop suddenly and can be severe within hours of onset
incubation_period.note: Shorter incubation (1–2 days) is common; distinguishes flu from many other respiratory infections with longer incubation periods

uncomplicated.definition: Influenza illness involving the upper respiratory tract and/or lower respiratory tract without evidence of complications
uncomplicated.symptoms: Fever, cough, sore throat, rhinitis, headache, myalgia, fatigue
uncomplicated.management: Outpatient supportive care; antiviral therapy for high-risk patients within 2 days of onset

complicated.definition: Influenza with evidence of lower respiratory tract disease, central nervous system involvement, significant dehydration, bacterial superinfection, or exacerbation of underlying chronic conditions
complicated.management: Hospitalization; antiviral therapy (oseltamivir preferred); monitor for secondary bacterial infection

severe.definition: Requiring ICU admission; respiratory failure; hemodynamic instability; multi-organ involvement
severe.management: ICU care; invasive mechanical ventilation if needed; corticosteroids only for specific indications; broad-spectrum antibiotics if secondary bacterial pneumonia

pathophysiology.overview: Influenza virus infects ciliated respiratory epithelial cells via hemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors. Viral replication destroys the epithelial lining, triggering innate immune responses. Systemic symptoms (fever, myalgia, fatigue) are primarily immune-mediated via cytokines rather than direct viral invasion of systemic tissues.

phase_1_infection_and_replication.description: Virus infects upper respiratory tract epithelium; incubation phase; innate immune activation begins; type I interferon (IFN-α/β) production initiated
phase_1_infection_and_replication.viral_tropism: Ciliated columnar epithelium of nasal passages, trachea, bronchi; type I and II pneumocytes in severe disease
phase_1_infection_and_replication.tissue_destruction: Viral replication destroys cilia and epithelial cells; impairs mucociliary clearance; creates portal for secondary bacterial infections

phase_2_immune_response.description: Innate immune response: neutrophils and macrophages infiltrate respiratory mucosa; cytokine production causes systemic symptoms
phase_2_immune_response.systemic_symptoms_mechanism: Cytokines (especially TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-α) cause fever, myalgia, fatigue, and headache — not direct viral invasion of muscles or brain
phase_2_immune_response.lymphocyte_response: T-cell and B-cell adaptive immunity develops within 5–10 days; antibodies to HA and NA key to clearance and protection

phase_3_complications.primary_viral_pneumonia: Direct viral pneumonia from influenza replication in alveolar epithelium; bilateral patchy infiltrates; high mortality; less common than secondary bacterial pneumonia
phase_3_complications.secondary_bacterial_pneumonia: Most common severe complication; destruction of ciliated epithelium allows bacterial colonization; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes most common organisms; may occur 3–7 days after initial improvement
phase_3_complications.cytokine_dysregulation: Severe influenza can trigger dysregulated cytokine response; exaggerated inflammatory response contributes to ARDS and multi-organ dysfunction
phase_3_complications.cardiovascular: Influenza infection triggers acute MI via plaque destabilization, hypercoagulable state, and direct myocardial inflammation; risk of MI increases 3–5x in week after flu diagnosis
phase_3_complications.neurological: Rare but includes encephalitis, acute necrotizing encephalopathy, febrile seizures; especially in children

common_symptoms: Sudden onset of fever or feeling feverish/chills (38–40°C / 100.4–104°F)
Severe muscle aches and body pains (myalgia)
Watery or red eyes (conjunctivitis — less common)
severe_symptoms: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Oxygen saturation below 92% on room air
Signs of dehydration (no urination for 8+ hours, dry mouth, dizziness)
Bluish discoloration of lips or fingernails (cyanosis)
High fever above 40°C (104°F) unresponsive to antipyretics
Severe weakness or inability to stand
In children: fast breathing or labored breathing, ribs showing with each breath, grayish skin color, not drinking fluids
Symptoms that improve then return with fever and worsening cough (sign of secondary bacterial pneumonia)
causes: Infection with influenza type A viruses (H1N1, H3N2 — responsible for most seasonal epidemics)
Infection with influenza type B viruses (B/Victoria lineage — primarily affects children and young adults)
Infection with influenza type C virus (mild, rare)
Zoonotic infection with avian influenza (H5N1, H7N9) from direct animal contact
Hemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors on respiratory epithelial cells initiating viral entry
Viral replication within ciliated respiratory epithelium causing cell death and inflammation
Cytokine-mediated systemic inflammatory response producing fever, myalgia, and fatigue
Antigenic drift enabling seasonal strain to evade pre-existing immunity from prior infection or vaccination

risk_factors.details: Highest hospitalization and death rates among infants <6 months; immature immune system; high-risk group for severe complications
All children under 5 considered at increased risk for serious flu complications; highest incidence of influenza illness
Immunosenescence; highest hospitalization and mortality rates; responsible for >90% of influenza deaths in the US; attenuated vaccine response

risk_factors.factor: Pregnancy (all trimesters) and up to 2 weeks postpartum
risk_factors.details: Physiological immunomodulation; reduced lung capacity; increased risk of hospitalization, ICU admission, preterm birth, and maternal death; influenza vaccination strongly recommended
Influenza triggers severe asthma and COPD exacerbations; impaired mucociliary clearance; high risk of pneumonia
Heart disease (excluding hypertension alone); influenza increases MI risk 3–5x; heart failure worsened by fluid shifts and hypoxemia
Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil and macrophage function; higher risk of secondary bacterial pneumonia and hospitalization
Uremia impairs immune function; higher complication and hospitalization rates
Impaired immune function and coagulation; higher risk of severe influenza
Includes cerebral palsy, epilepsy, stroke, intellectual disability, muscular dystrophy, spinal cord injury; impaired airway clearance; higher aspiration risk
Vascular and pulmonary complications worsened by influenza infection; high-risk group per CDC/IDSA
Obesity (BMI ≥ 40 — morbid obesity) significantly increases risk of severe influenza and hospitalization; impaired respiratory mechanics; pro-inflammatory state

HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, cancer patients on chemotherapy, patients on high-dose corticosteroids or biological therapies; markedly impaired influenza-specific immunity; higher viral loads and prolonged shedding
Strongest modifiable risk factor for influenza-related hospitalization and death; annual vaccination significantly reduces risk

risk_factors.factor: Residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities
risk_factors.details: High concentration of elderly and frail individuals; close quarters facilitate rapid spread; institutional outbreaks common

risk_factors.factor: Children aged <19 years on long-term aspirin therapy
risk_factors.details: Risk of Reye's syndrome if given aspirin during influenza infection; aspirin must be avoided; acetaminophen or ibuprofen preferred
Higher hospitalization rates for influenza compared to white populations; CDC high-priority group for vaccination
Damages respiratory epithelium and cilia; impairs mucociliary clearance; increases severity of influenza

diagnosis_methods.description: Detects influenza A and B viral nucleoprotein antigens in respiratory specimens; results in 10–15 minutes
diagnosis_methods.specimen: Nasopharyngeal swab, nasal swab, or nasal wash
diagnosis_methods.sensitivity: 50–70% (variable; low sensitivity means negative results do not exclude flu)
diagnosis_methods.who_2024_recommendation: Digital immunoassay (DIA) preferred over traditional RIDTs for non-severe cases; DIA has higher sensitivity (~80%) than traditional RIDTs
diagnosis_methods.limitation: Cannot distinguish influenza subtypes; negative result does not rule out flu — treat based on clinical judgment

diagnosis_methods.method: RT-PCR (Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction) / NAAT
diagnosis_methods.description: Detects influenza viral RNA; most sensitive and specific test; can identify and subtype influenza A and B; can distinguish seasonal from pandemic strains
diagnosis_methods.specimen: Nasopharyngeal swab (reference standard); nasal swab; bronchoalveolar lavage in severe disease
diagnosis_methods.turnaround_time: 2–8 hours in laboratory; 30–60 minutes for point-of-care platforms
diagnosis_methods.who_2024_recommendation: NAAT recommended for diagnosing suspected SEVERE influenza and for all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza

diagnosis_methods.description: Simultaneously tests for influenza A, influenza B, and other respiratory pathogens (RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, adenovirus, etc.) in one assay
diagnosis_methods.clinical_role: Preferred for hospitalized patients; differentiates influenza from COVID-19 and other co-circulating respiratory viruses
diagnosis_methods.authority: CDC and IDSA recommend for hospitalized patients with severe respiratory illness

diagnosis_methods.description: Detects influenza viral antigens in respiratory epithelial cells using fluorescently labelled antibodies; distinguishes influenza A and B
diagnosis_methods.clinical_role: Useful when rapid PCR not available; less commonly used now

diagnosis_methods.description: Gold standard for virus isolation and characterization; grows live virus in cell culture (MDCK cells) or embryonated eggs
diagnosis_methods.clinical_role: Not used for acute diagnosis; used for public health surveillance, antiviral resistance testing, vaccine strain selection
diagnosis_methods.authority: WHO GISRS (Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System) uses viral culture for global monitoring

diagnosis_methods.description: Detects influenza-specific antibodies (paired acute and convalescent serum showing ≥4-fold rise in HI titer confirms infection)
diagnosis_methods.timing: Requires 2 serum samples taken 2–4 weeks apart; not useful for acute diagnosis
diagnosis_methods.clinical_role: Epidemiological surveillance; research; not for acute clinical diagnosis

diagnosis_methods.description: Reveals bilateral patchy infiltrates or consolidation in influenza pneumonia; may be normal in uncomplicated influenza
diagnosis_methods.clinical_role: Indicated for patients with dyspnea, hypoxemia, or suspected pneumonia; not needed for uncomplicated flu
diagnosis_methods.finding: Bilateral interstitial or patchy alveolar infiltrates; lobar consolidation if secondary bacterial pneumonia

diagnosis_methods.description: Reveals leukopenia (low white cell count) and lymphopenia in uncomplicated influenza; leukocytosis with neutrophilia suggests secondary bacterial infection

typical_findings.WBC: Normal or low (leukopenia in early viral phase)
typical_findings.note: High WBC/neutrophilia should raise suspicion of bacterial superinfection

diagnosis_methods.description: Used to assess severity in hospitalized patients

key_markers.CRP: Elevated in influenza pneumonia; very high CRP suggests secondary bacterial infection
key_markers.procalcitonin: Low/normal in pure viral influenza; elevated if bacterial superinfection; helps guide antibiotic decisions
key_markers.LDH: Elevated in severe influenza with extensive tissue destruction

diagnosis_methods.description: Monitors peripheral oxygen saturation; SpO2 < 92% indicates significant hypoxemia; home monitoring recommended in high-risk patients
diagnosis_methods.clinical_importance: Identify early respiratory decompensation; guide oxygen supplementation

treatment_options.description: Most healthy adults and children recover from uncomplicated influenza with supportive care only
interventions: Rest and avoid strenuous activity during febrile illness
Stay home to prevent spread to others
Adequate hydration — water, broths, herbal teas, oral rehydration solutions (2–3 liters daily)
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen for fever, headache, and myalgia — NOT aspirin (except adults; never in children due to Reye's syndrome risk)
Warm saline gargles for sore throat
Nasal decongestants or saline nasal rinse for congestion
Honey and warm fluids for cough (adults and children over 1 year)
Monitor for worsening; seek care if symptoms do not improve after 5 days or worsen

treatment_options.description: Patients with risk factors for severe disease should receive antiviral therapy as early as possible — within 2 days of symptom onset for best effect
interventions: Oral oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — preferred for high-risk outpatients with suspected/confirmed influenza
Oral baloxavir marboxil (Xofluza) — conditionally recommended within 2 days for high-risk patients (WHO 2024)
Inhaled zanamivir or IV peramivir as alternatives based on age and contraindications (CDC 2025)
Supportive care as above
Close monitoring for complications
Antiviral treatment recommended even if >48 hours since symptom onset in high-risk patients with progressive disease (CDC)

treatment_options.setting: Complicated — Hospitalized with Pneumonia or Lower Respiratory Involvement
treatment_options.description: Patients with complications require hospital admission and aggressive treatment
interventions: IV oseltamivir or oral oseltamivir (preferred antiviral; start regardless of time since symptom onset)
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 94%
IV fluids if dehydrated or unable to take orally
Antibiotics if secondary bacterial pneumonia suspected (based on WBC, procalcitonin, CXR consolidation) — amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftriaxone, or based on local antibiogram
Blood cultures and sputum cultures before antibiotics
Monitor inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin, CBC) daily
Deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis (LMWH)

treatment_options.description: Patients with respiratory failure, ARDS, or hemodynamic instability require intensive care
interventions: IV oseltamivir 75–150 mg twice daily (higher dose considered in severe disease)
Invasive mechanical ventilation for ARDS (lung-protective: low tidal volume 6 mL/kg IBW)
High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) or NIV as bridge before intubation
Prone positioning for severe ARDS
Vasopressors for septic shock
Corticosteroids only for ARDS per WHO 2024 recommendations (NOT recommended routinely; may worsen outcomes)
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for secondary bacterial pneumonia (Staphylococcal MRSA coverage if needed)
ECMO for refractory ARDS in specialized centers
Renal replacement therapy for AKI

treatment_options.description: Antivirals can prevent influenza after exposure — recommended for high-risk individuals exposed within 48 hours
interventions: Oseltamivir 75 mg once daily for 10 days post-exposure (WHO 2024 conditional recommendation for high-risk individuals)
Baloxavir, zanamivir, or laninamivir as alternatives (WHO 2024)
Not recommended for routine use or as a substitute for vaccination
Consider for unvaccinated high-risk individuals exposed to confirmed influenza within 48 hours
Institutional outbreak management: treat all residents/staff with antivirals (CDC/IDSA)

medications.name: Oseltamivir
medications.mechanism: Inhibits influenza A and B neuraminidase, preventing release of newly formed virions from infected cells and reducing viral spread through the respiratory tract
medications.indication: Treatment of acute uncomplicated influenza in patients ≥2 weeks of age; high-risk outpatients; hospitalized patients; post-exposure prophylaxis

dosing.adult_severe: 75–150 mg twice daily for 5–10 days (extended course for hospitalized/ICU)
dosing.pediatric: Weight-based dosing from 2 weeks to <1 year; age/weight-based for older children
dosing.prophylaxis: 75 mg once daily for 10 days (post-exposure) or up to 6 weeks (seasonal)

medications.treatment_window: Most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset; still recommended after 48 hours in high-risk or hospitalized patients
medications.authority: WHO preferred for severe influenza; CDC preferred; IDSA recommended; WHO 2024 — conditionally recommended for severe influenza
medications.pregnancy: Preferred antiviral for pregnant and breastfeeding women; oseltamivir safety data robust
medications.resistance: H275Y mutation in neuraminidase confers high-level oseltamivir resistance; limited but monitor via surveillance

medications.name: Baloxavir Marboxil
medications.mechanism: Inhibits the PB2 cap-binding subunit of viral RNA polymerase; blocks viral mRNA synthesis at a different step than neuraminidase inhibitors; single-dose regimen
medications.indication: Treatment of uncomplicated influenza A and B in patients ≥5 years; post-exposure prophylaxis

dosing.adult_treatment: 40 mg single dose (for patients <80 kg); 80 mg single dose (≥80 kg)

medications.authority: WHO 2024 conditionally recommends for high-risk non-severe cases; CDC includes as option; approved by FDA for treatment and prophylaxis
medications.advantage: Single oral dose improves adherence; novel mechanism — effective against oseltamivir-resistant strains
medications.concern: Post-treatment resistance mutations reported (I38T); not recommended in pregnancy (insufficient safety data)

medications.name: Zanamivir
medications.mechanism: Inhibits influenza A and B neuraminidase; structurally similar to sialic acid
medications.route: Inhaled (dry powder inhaler); IV formulation available for compassionate use in severe cases
medications.indication: Treatment of uncomplicated influenza A and B in patients ≥7 years; prophylaxis in patients ≥5 years

dosing.treatment: 10 mg (two 5 mg inhalations) twice daily for 5 days
dosing.prophylaxis: 10 mg once daily for 10 days (post-exposure) or 28 days (seasonal)

medications.contraindications: Inhaled form contraindicated in patients with asthma or COPD (may cause bronchospasm); not recommended in pregnancy unless benefits outweigh risks
medications.authority: CDC: option for outpatient treatment; WHO 2024: alternative for prophylaxis

medications.name: Peramivir
medications.mechanism: IV neuraminidase inhibitor; same class as oseltamivir and zanamivir
medications.indication: Treatment of acute uncomplicated influenza in adults and children ≥2 years; useful when oral route not available

dosing.adult: 600 mg single IV dose over 15–30 minutes

medications.advantage: Single IV dose; useful for hospitalized patients who cannot take oral medications
medications.authority: CDC includes as treatment option; FDA approved

medications.name: Amantadine / Rimantadine
medications.mechanism: Blocks M2 ion channel of influenza A, preventing viral uncoating
medications.current_status: NOT recommended for treatment or prophylaxis of influenza A due to widespread resistance (>99% of circulating H3N2 and H1N1pdm09 strains resistant)
medications.historical_use: Previously used for influenza A; resistance emerged rapidly in 2000s
medications.note: No activity against influenza B; not useful for current circulating strains

medications.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen
medications.mechanism: Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis in CNS; reduces fever and pain
medications.indication: First-line symptomatic treatment of fever, headache, and myalgia in influenza
medications.dosing_adult: 500–1000 mg every 4–6 hours; maximum 4000 mg/day (3000 mg/day with liver disease)
medications.notes: PREFERRED over aspirin in all patients under 18 years (Reye's syndrome risk); preferred in pregnancy; safe OTC option

medications.name: Ibuprofen
medications.mechanism: Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2; reduces prostaglandin synthesis; antipyretic, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory
medications.indication: Alternative to paracetamol for fever, myalgia, and headache in influenza
medications.dosing_adult: 400–600 mg every 6–8 hours with food; max 2400 mg/day
medications.notes: Avoid in children <6 months; avoid in pregnancy (3rd trimester); avoid in renal impairment; good option for adults

medications.name: Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic acid)
medications.warning: NEVER use aspirin or aspirin-containing products in children or adolescents with influenza — causes Reye's syndrome (rare but life-threatening hepatic encephalopathy). Paracetamol or ibuprofen must be used instead.
medications.note: Children aged <19 years on long-term aspirin therapy are a high-risk group; requires antiviral therapy if they develop influenza

medications.name: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (for secondary bacterial pneumonia)
medications.indication: Secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza; NOT for uncomplicated influenza (viral infection; antibiotics ineffective)
medications.authority: CDC, IDSA: antibiotics only for confirmed or highly suspected bacterial superinfection

fever.description: Rapid onset high fever 38–40°C (100.4–104°F); may be accompanied by rigors (shaking chills); highly characteristic of flu vs cold
fever.onset: Abrupt; often can pinpoint exact hour symptoms began — hallmark of influenza
fever.management: Paracetamol or ibuprofen; never aspirin in children; cool compresses; adequate hydration

myalgia.description: Severe muscle aches, particularly in legs, back, and upper arms; often the most debilitating symptom; makes movement painful
myalgia.mechanism: Cytokine-mediated (TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-α) — not direct viral invasion of muscles
myalgia.management: Paracetamol or ibuprofen; rest; warm bath may provide temporary relief

cough.description: Initially dry, non-productive; may progress to productive cough if secondary bacterial infection develops
cough.management: Honey and warm liquids; humidifier; cough suppressants (dextromethorphan) for adults with severe dry cough

headache.description: Often severe frontal headache; typically bilateral; may be accompanied by photophobia; cytokine-mediated
headache.management: Paracetamol or ibuprofen; dark room rest; adequate hydration

fatigue.description: Profound weakness and tiredness often disproportionate to other symptoms; can persist weeks after acute illness (post-influenza fatigue syndrome)
fatigue.recovery: Most resolve within 2 weeks; some experience post-viral fatigue for 4–6 weeks, especially elderly

loss_of_appetite.description: Reduced appetite common during acute febrile illness; contributes to dehydration risk
loss_of_appetite.management: Small, frequent light meals; nutrient-dense foods even with low appetite; focus on hydration above solid food intake

gastrointestinal_symptoms.description: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea less common in seasonal influenza but more prominent in children and with influenza B; stomach flu is NOT influenza
gastrointestinal_symptoms.clarification: 'Stomach flu' is a misnomer — true influenza is a respiratory disease; GI illnesses are caused by other pathogens (norovirus, rotavirus)

lifestyle_home_remedies.remedy: Complete bed rest during acute febrile phase
lifestyle_home_remedies.details: Reduce physical activity until fever-free without antipyretics for at least 24 hours; rest conserves immune energy; avoid return to work, school, or public places while symptomatic to prevent spread

2–3 liters of fluid daily; fever and sweating cause significant fluid loss; monitor for dehydration signs (dark urine, no urination for 8+ hours, dry mouth, dizziness); oral rehydration solutions if vomiting

lifestyle_home_remedies.evidence: Moderate — traditional and some clinical evidence
lifestyle_home_remedies.details: Provides hydration, electrolytes (sodium, potassium), protein (antibody production), and zinc; steam helps clear nasal congestion; anti-inflammatory compounds in chicken broth; classic evidence-based flu remedy
lifestyle_home_remedies.authority: Supported by observational research; endorsed by most clinical guides

lifestyle_home_remedies.details: 1/4–1/2 teaspoon salt in 8 oz warm water; gargle 30 seconds 3–4x daily; soothes sore throat; reduces pharyngeal inflammation; does not have antiviral properties but improves comfort

Inhaling steam or using a cool-mist humidifier loosens nasal and chest congestion; adds moisture to irritated airways; no antiviral benefit but significant symptom relief; caution with young children (burn risk from steam)
1–2 teaspoons honey in warm water or herbal tea; reduces cough frequency and severity; safe for adults and children over 1 year; never for infants <1 year (botulism risk)
lifestyle_home_remedies.authority: WHO and NICE recommend honey as first-line treatment for cough in adults and children

lifestyle_home_remedies.details: Commercial saline nasal spray or neti pot with distilled/boiled water; flushes viral particles and mucus from nasal passages; reduces congestion; recommended 2–3 times daily

Topical menthol/eucalyptus preparations on chest and throat create cooling sensation that reduces subjective nasal congestion; not recommended for children under 2 years on face or near nostrils; adult formula only

lifestyle_home_remedies.evidence: Strong for reducing viral load in room
lifestyle_home_remedies.details: Open windows for fresh air circulation; avoid recirculating air in sick room; use HEPA air purifiers if available; reduces viral particle concentration for household members

Stay home for at least 24 hours after fever has resolved without fever-reducing medications; wear a surgical mask in shared spaces; designate separate bathroom if possible; disinfect high-touch surfaces daily
Fresh ginger (1 inch), honey (1 tsp), lemon juice in hot water; ginger reduces nausea, has anti-inflammatory properties (6-gingerol, 6-shogaol); honey soothes throat; lemon provides vitamin C
7–9 hours per night; cytokine production and T-cell activity peak during deep sleep; sleep deprivation during illness prolongs recovery and increases complication risk
Smoking worsens respiratory tract inflammation; impairs mucociliary clearance; significantly increases risk of influenza pneumonia and complications; complete smoking cessation recommended

lifestyle_home_remedies.remedy: Warm compresses for headache and myalgia
lifestyle_home_remedies.details: Warm compress on forehead or neck for headache; warm towel or heating pad on aching muscles for myalgia relief; combine with paracetamol or ibuprofen for best effect

examples: Chicken soup (classic; zinc, protein, N-acetylcysteine-like compounds)
diet_recommended.mechanism: Hydration; electrolyte replacement; steam clears nasal passages; anti-inflammatory compounds; easy to digest with low appetite; warmth soothes sore throat
Vitamin C supports neutrophil function, lymphocyte production, and antibody synthesis; antioxidant effect reduces oxidative stress from infection; may reduce duration of symptoms

diet_recommended.evidence: Moderate — meta-analysis shows vitamin D reduces flu infection risk
diet_recommended.mechanism: Vitamin D activates innate immune response; promotes production of antimicrobial peptides (cathelicidins); deficiency strongly associated with increased flu susceptibility
Zinc inhibits viral replication; essential for T-cell and NK cell function; zinc deficiency impairs antiviral immunity
6-gingerol and 6-shogaol have anti-inflammatory, antiviral, and antiemetic properties; reduces nausea and vomiting; soothes sore throat and cough

diet_recommended.evidence: Strong for cough and sore throat
diet_recommended.mechanism: Antiviral and antimicrobial properties (hydrogen peroxide, methylglyoxal); demulcent effect coats throat; anti-inflammatory; WHO-endorsed for cough relief

diet_recommended.evidence: Moderate — traditional and some clinical evidence
diet_recommended.mechanism: Allicin (active compound) has antiviral and immunomodulatory properties; may reduce severity and duration of flu; anti-inflammatory

diet_recommended.evidence: Emerging — gut microbiome linked to immune response
diet_recommended.mechanism: Maintains gut microbiome diversity; gut-immune axis supports respiratory immunity; some studies show probiotics reduce flu severity
Protein required for antibody production, immune cell synthesis, and tissue repair; fever increases protein catabolism; maintain 0.8–1.2g/kg daily
Replaces electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) lost through fever, sweating; prevents and treats dehydration; critical for recovery
Curcumin inhibits NF-κB inflammatory pathway; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; may reduce cytokine-driven symptoms

diet_to_avoid.evidence: Very strong; significantly suppresses immunity and worsens outcomes
diet_to_avoid.details: Heavy alcohol use is a risk factor for severe influenza and complications; suppresses innate and adaptive immunity; impairs mucociliary clearance; causes dehydration; increases pneumonia risk; complete abstinence recommended during illness
diet_to_avoid.authority: CDC cites heavy alcohol use as a risk factor for severe influenza outcomes

diet_to_avoid.mechanism: Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil phagocytic activity; high sugar intake promotes inflammation; little nutritional value; worsens dehydration (osmotic effect)

diet_to_avoid.evidence: Strong — pro-inflammatory and hard to digest
diet_to_avoid.mechanism: High in trans fats and refined carbohydrates; pro-inflammatory; hard to digest when appetite is reduced; displace nutrient-dense foods
Pro-inflammatory; high sodium; nitrates and nitrites; minimal nutritional benefit during illness

diet_to_avoid.details: Some people find cold dairy (cold milk, ice cream) increases mucus thickness or worsens congestion. If this is your personal experience, temporarily reduce; no strong clinical evidence to universally avoid dairy — yogurt with probiotics is recommended
diet_to_avoid.nuance: Warm dairy (warm milk) is fine; avoid ice cream and cold milk if mucus worsens

diet_to_avoid.details: Coffee and strong tea cause mild diuresis; can worsen dehydration during flu; also disrupts sleep which is critical for immune recovery; limit to 1 cup of tea or coffee per day during illness
diet_to_avoid.exception: Herbal teas (ginger, chamomile, peppermint) without caffeine are strongly recommended

diet_to_avoid.details: Smoking impairs mucociliary clearance; destroys respiratory epithelium; dramatically increases risk of influenza pneumonia and complications; strongly increases secondary bacterial infection risk; complete cessation recommended

Aspirin or aspirin-containing products (including some cold/flu medications) MUST NEVER be given to children or adolescents with influenza — causes Reye's syndrome (life-threatening liver failure and brain swelling). Always use paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen instead. Check all OTC flu medication labels for salicylate content.

Nausea is common with flu; heavy meals cause digestive discomfort; stick to small, light, easily digestible meals; avoid fried foods, rich sauces, red meat in large portions; soups, broths, and soft foods preferred

complications.name: Primary Viral Pneumonia
complications.description: Direct extension of influenza virus into lower respiratory tract (alveoli); bilateral patchy infiltrates; high mortality; more common with pandemic strains; less common than secondary bacterial pneumonia

complications.name: Secondary Bacterial Pneumonia
complications.description: Most common severe complication; influenza destroys ciliated epithelium creating portal for bacterial infection 3–7 days after initial viral illness; classic pattern: initial improvement then relapse with worsening fever and productive cough; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes most common organisms
complications.note: MRSA co-infection particularly dangerous; high mortality

complications.name: Mixed Viral-Bacterial Pneumonia
complications.description: Simultaneous viral and bacterial pneumonia; combination of both patterns; significant mortality

complications.name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
complications.description: Bilateral lung injury with refractory hypoxemia; complication of severe viral or secondary bacterial pneumonia; requires ICU and mechanical ventilation

complications.name: Exacerbation of Asthma
complications.description: Influenza is the most common trigger of severe asthma exacerbations; can require emergency hospitalization

complications.name: Exacerbation of COPD
complications.description: Influenza triggers acute COPD exacerbations with increased mucus, bronchospasm, and hypoxemia

complications.name: Croup (in children)
complications.description: Influenza A and B are common causes of viral croup in children; laryngotracheobronchitis with characteristic barking cough and stridor

complications.name: Acute Myocardial Infarction (MI)
complications.description: Influenza infection increases MI risk 3–5x in the week following diagnosis; mechanisms include plaque destabilization, hypercoagulable state, direct cardiac inflammation, and hypoxemia-induced demand ischemia
complications.prevention: Influenza vaccination significantly reduces risk of MI in high-risk cardiac patients

complications.name: Myocarditis and Pericarditis
complications.description: Rare; direct viral inflammation of heart muscle; presents with chest pain, elevated troponin, ECG changes

complications.name: Worsening of Congestive Heart Failure
complications.description: Influenza triggers acute decompensated heart failure in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease

complications.name: Febrile Seizures
complications.description: Most common neurological complication in children aged 6 months to 5 years; high fever triggers seizure; usually benign and self-limiting

complications.name: Influenza-Associated Encephalitis / Encephalopathy
complications.description: Rare but serious; altered consciousness, seizures, behavioral changes; can occur without direct viral brain invasion; cytokine-mediated; acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE) in children

complications.name: Reye's Syndrome
complications.description: Rare but life-threatening hepatic encephalopathy in children given aspirin during viral illness (especially influenza or varicella); presents with vomiting, confusion, liver failure; prevented by avoiding aspirin in children
complications.prevention: Complete avoidance of aspirin in patients under 18 years with suspected viral illness

complications.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
complications.description: Rare post-infectious autoimmune peripheral neuropathy; ascending muscle weakness; can follow influenza infection

complications.name: Otitis Media (Ear Infection)
complications.description: Very common in children with influenza; bacteria colonize Eustachian tube after viral damage; ear pain, hearing loss; treated with antibiotics if bacterial

complications.name: Sinusitis
complications.description: Secondary bacterial sinusitis following influenza; nasal congestion → sinus obstruction → bacterial overgrowth; facial pain, purulent discharge

complications.name: Post-Influenza Fatigue Syndrome
complications.description: Persistent fatigue, weakness, and malaise lasting weeks to months after acute influenza; more common in elderly; impairs return to normal activity

raw_source_backup.when_to_see_doctor: Seek medical evaluation promptly if you are in a high-risk group (age ≥65, child <5 years, pregnant, immunocompromised, or have chronic heart, lung, kidney, liver, metabolic, or neurological conditions) and develop flu symptoms — early antiviral treatment within 48 hours significantly reduces severity. You should also see a doctor if symptoms are unusually severe from onset, if you are not improving after 5 days, if fever returns after initial improvement (possible secondary bacterial pneumonia), if you develop difficulty breathing, or if you are unsure whether you need antiviral treatment. Patients with asthma or COPD should contact their doctor immediately as influenza triggers severe exacerbations requiring urgent medication adjustment.

Confusion, disorientation, or altered mental status

Seizures

High fever above 40°C (104°F) unresponsive to paracetamol or ibuprofen

vaccination.overview: Annual influenza vaccination is the single most effective strategy to prevent influenza illness, hospitalization, and death. Vaccines are reformulated each year to match predicted circulating strains.
vaccination.who_should_get_vaccinated: Everyone aged ≥6 months (CDC 2025); priority groups include elderly (≥65), children (6 months–5 years), pregnant women, healthcare workers, immunocompromised individuals, and people with chronic medical conditions
vaccination.timing: Ideally before the start of flu season (by end of October in northern hemisphere); vaccination at any time during flu season still beneficial

vaccine_types.notes: Standard recommendation for most people including pregnant women and immunocompromised

vaccine_types.notes: Alternative to high-dose for adults ≥65 years

vaccine_types.notes: Safe for egg-allergic individuals; preferred by some clinicians for immunocompromised

vaccine_types.mechanism: Contains weakened live virus; administered intranasally; stimulates both mucosal and systemic immunity; may provide broader immune response
contraindications: Children 2–4 with wheezing or asthma history

vaccination.vaccine_composition: Quadrivalent vaccines contain two influenza A strains (H1N1 and H3N2) and one or two influenza B strains; selected by WHO GISRS twice yearly (February for northern hemisphere; September for southern hemisphere) based on circulating strains

vaccine_effectiveness.typical_range: 40–60% against influenza A; higher against influenza B
vaccine_effectiveness.variability: Depends on match between vaccine strains and circulating strains; higher in well-matched seasons
vaccine_effectiveness.severe_disease: More effective at preventing hospitalization and death (70–85%) than preventing all symptomatic illness
vaccine_effectiveness.cardiovascular_benefit: Vaccination reduces risk of MI by 15–30% in high-risk cardiac patients (multiple studies)

Baloxavir (single dose or repeated dosing — under study)

Institutional outbreaks in nursing homes — treat all residents and staff
Immunocompromised individuals who may not respond to vaccination
Pregnant women in high-transmission settings when vaccination contraindicated

non_pharmaceutical_interventions.evidence: Very strong — single most effective preventive measure
non_pharmaceutical_interventions.details: All persons ≥6 months annually; priority for high-risk groups
Wash hands with soap and water for ≥20 seconds especially after coughing/sneezing, before eating, after touching surfaces in public; use alcohol-based sanitizer (≥60% ethanol) when soap unavailable
Cover mouth and nose with tissue or inner elbow when coughing or sneezing; discard tissue immediately; wash hands; reduces droplet spread
Stay home for at least 24 hours after fever has resolved without fever-reducing medications; reduces community transmission; critical for preventing spread in workplaces and schools

non_pharmaceutical_interventions.measure: Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth
non_pharmaceutical_interventions.details: Reduces fomite transmission; influenza virus survives on surfaces up to 24 hours
Surgical mask or N95 respirator reduces influenza transmission; especially recommended for healthcare workers, high-risk patients in crowded settings during peak flu season

Increase outdoor air ventilation in schools, workplaces, and healthcare settings; HEPA air purifiers; CO2 monitoring

non_pharmaceutical_interventions.measure: Avoid close contact with sick people
non_pharmaceutical_interventions.details: Maintain distance from people with flu symptoms; especially important for high-risk individuals

Enhanced infection control measures (hand hygiene, PPE, visitor restrictions)

Teach proper isolation technique to prevent household transmission
Ensure patient understands medication schedule (antivirals, antipyretics)
Assess hydration status at each contact; reinforce fluid intake targets
Remind about Reye's syndrome risk — confirm NO aspirin for children
Telehealth or phone follow-up for high-risk patients within 24–48 hours
Mental health and social support — isolation is distressing; especially for elderly living alone
hospitalized_moderate: Vital signs monitoring every 4–8 hours (temperature, HR, RR, BP, SpO2)
Administer antiviral medications on schedule (oseltamivir — with food to reduce nausea)
Administer antipyretics as prescribed; tepid sponging for high fever
Monitor blood glucose in diabetic patients (fever and illness cause hyperglycemia)
Respiratory assessment — listen for new crackles or decreased breath sounds (bacterial pneumonia)
Obtain blood cultures and sputum cultures before antibiotics if bacterial superinfection suspected
Infection control: droplet precautions, hand hygiene, patient education on cough hygiene
Nutritional support — small, frequent meals; enteral nutrition if oral intake insufficient
DVT prophylaxis (LMWH) for hospitalized patients with immobility
icu_severe: Continuous cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, and respiratory rate monitoring
Arterial line for continuous blood pressure monitoring and ABG sampling
Invasive mechanical ventilation management — low tidal volume (6 mL/kg IBW), PEEP titration
Prone positioning protocols for severe ARDS (team of ≥4 staff; 12–16 hours/day)
Strict infection control — N95 for AGPs; droplet precautions standard
Pressure ulcer prevention — repositioning every 2 hours
Family communication — ICU visiting restrictions; provide regular updates

transmission_precautions.contact: Gloves + gown; hand hygiene before and after all patient contacts

environmental: Single-room isolation if available; otherwise cohort influenza patients
Negative pressure room for high-risk aerosol-generating procedures if available
Daily disinfection of high-touch surfaces with hospital-grade disinfectant
Adequate ventilation (≥6 air changes per hour for influenza isolation rooms)

Leukopenia (very low WBC) OR leukocytosis (suggesting bacterial superinfection)
