faq.question: What is influenza (flu)?
faq.answer: Influenza (flu) is a highly contagious acute respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses (A, B, C, D). It primarily affects the nose, throat, and lungs, causing sudden onset of fever, severe muscle aches, headache, cough, and fatigue. It is not the same as the common cold — flu is generally more severe and has an abrupt onset.

faq.question: How does flu spread?
faq.answer: Flu spreads mainly through respiratory droplets expelled when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. It can also spread through aerosols in enclosed poorly ventilated spaces, and by touching contaminated surfaces then touching the nose, mouth, or eyes.

faq.question: What are the symptoms of flu?
faq.answer: Flu symptoms appear suddenly and include high fever or chills, severe muscle aches, severe headache, dry cough, sore throat, fatigue, and nasal congestion or runny nose. Loss of appetite and watery eyes are also common. Flu is distinguished from a cold by its abrupt onset and severity of systemic symptoms.

faq.question: What is the incubation period of flu?
faq.answer: The incubation period is 1–4 days, most commonly about 2 days. Flu has an abrupt onset — most people can identify the exact time symptoms began, unlike the gradual onset of a cold.

faq.question: How is flu diagnosed?
faq.answer: Flu can be diagnosed clinically based on typical symptoms during flu season. Rapid antigen tests give results in 15 minutes but have limited sensitivity. Digital immunoassay (DIA) is preferred for non-severe cases. RT-PCR/NAAT is recommended for hospitalized patients and severe illness — it is the most accurate test.

faq.question: What is the treatment for flu?
faq.answer: Uncomplicated flu in healthy individuals is managed with rest, hydration, and antipyretics (paracetamol or ibuprofen — never aspirin in children). High-risk patients and those with severe disease should receive antiviral medications (oseltamivir, baloxavir, zanamivir, or peramivir) within 48 hours of symptom onset for best effect.

faq.question: What is oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and who should take it?
faq.answer: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is an oral neuraminidase inhibitor antiviral medication that reduces flu severity and duration when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. It is recommended for all hospitalized flu patients, high-risk patients (elderly, pregnant, immunocompromised, chronic disease), and children under 2 years. It is also used for post-exposure prophylaxis.

faq.question: Can antibiotics treat flu?
faq.answer: No. Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics should NOT be given for uncomplicated influenza. However, if flu is complicated by secondary bacterial pneumonia (most common severe complication), antibiotics are then appropriate and urgent.

faq.question: What is the difference between flu and a cold?
faq.answer: Flu has an abrupt onset and causes severe systemic symptoms — high fever, severe muscle aches, extreme fatigue, and headache. Cold symptoms develop gradually and are milder — runny nose, sore throat, sneezing, with little or no fever. Flu can cause life-threatening complications; colds rarely do.

faq.question: Who is at highest risk for severe flu?
faq.answer: Highest risk groups: adults ≥65 years, children <2 years (especially infants <6 months), pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals, people with chronic heart, lung, kidney, liver, or metabolic diseases, morbidly obese individuals (BMI ≥40), residents of nursing homes, and American Indians/Alaska Natives.

faq.question: What are the emergency signs of flu?
faq.answer: Emergency signs requiring immediate medical attention: difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion or altered mental status, severe vomiting preventing any fluid intake, cyanosis (blue lips or nails), seizures, extreme weakness, high fever above 40°C not responding to medication, and in children: ribs showing with each breath, grunting, inability to be wakened.

faq.question: How can I prevent flu?
faq.answer: Annual influenza vaccination is the most effective prevention strategy — recommended for everyone ≥6 months. Additional measures: frequent handwashing, covering coughs and sneezes, staying home when sick, avoiding close contact with sick people, and improving indoor ventilation. Post-exposure antivirals (oseltamivir) can be given to high-risk individuals exposed within 48 hours.

faq.question: Why do I need a flu vaccine every year?
faq.answer: Influenza viruses constantly mutate (antigenic drift), changing their surface proteins enough to partially evade the immunity built by prior infection or vaccination. The WHO reformulates the vaccine twice annually to match the predicted circulating strains. Additionally, vaccine-induced immunity wanes over time, making annual revaccination essential.

faq.question: What types of flu vaccine are available?
faq.answer: The main types: standard inactivated (injected; all ages ≥6 months), high-dose inactivated (recommended for ≥65 years), adjuvanted inactivated (for ≥65 years), recombinant (egg-free; for ≥18 years), and live attenuated nasal spray (FluMist; for healthy non-pregnant individuals aged 2–49 years). Quadrivalent vaccines cover two A and two B strains.

faq.question: Can pregnant women take antiviral medication for flu?
faq.answer: Yes — oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is the preferred antiviral for pregnant women with influenza, with extensive safety and efficacy data. Treatment should be started immediately, within 48 hours of symptom onset, without waiting for test confirmation. Aspirin must be avoided; paracetamol is used for fever. Influenza vaccination is also strongly recommended in all trimesters.

faq.question: Is flu dangerous for children?
faq.answer: Yes. All children under 5 are at increased risk for serious flu complications, with infants under 6 months at highest risk. Complications include pneumonia, otitis media, febrile seizures, and rarely encephalopathy. Children should be vaccinated annually from 6 months of age. Antivirals are recommended for hospitalized children, those under 2, and children with high-risk conditions. NEVER give aspirin to children with flu.

faq.question: What is the difference between influenza A and influenza B?
faq.answer: Influenza A is more clinically significant, infects humans and animals, causes more severe disease, and is responsible for all influenza pandemics. It is classified by HA and NA subtypes (H1N1, H3N2, etc.). Influenza B primarily infects humans, causes milder but still clinically significant disease, affects children more than adults, and does not cause pandemics. Both are covered by seasonal flu vaccines.

faq.question: What is antigenic drift and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Antigenic drift is the gradual accumulation of random mutations in the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) genes of influenza viruses during replication. These changes allow the virus to partially evade antibodies from prior infection or vaccination. This is why flu vaccines must be updated every year and why you can get the flu multiple times throughout life.

faq.question: What foods should I eat when I have the flu?
faq.answer: Focus on warm soups and broths (hydration and nutrients), vitamin C-rich fruits (oranges, kiwi, bell peppers), vitamin D foods (fatty fish, fortified milk), zinc-rich foods (legumes, pumpkin seeds), ginger and honey tea (anti-inflammatory and cough relief), and adequate fluids (2–3 liters daily). Small, frequent, easily digestible meals are preferred.

faq.question: What foods should I avoid during flu?
faq.answer: Avoid alcohol (suppresses immunity and causes dehydration), refined sugars (impair neutrophil function), ultra-processed and fried foods (pro-inflammatory, hard to digest), and excessive caffeine (worsens dehydration and disrupts sleep). Never give aspirin to children with flu — Reye's syndrome risk.
